reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation / Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
clinicalPearls: A rare, disabling disorder in which soft tissues progressively turn to bone through heterotopic endochondral ossification
Caused by a recurrent gain-of-function variant in ACVR1, a bone morphogenetic protein type I receptor, inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern but usually arising de novo
Characteristic malformed great toes present at birth are a vital early clue that often precedes any ossification
Painful soft-tissue flare-ups, sometimes triggered by trauma, injections, or viral illness, herald new bone formation, so biopsy and intramuscular injections should be avoided
Ossification typically progresses in a defined pattern, from axial to appendicular and cranial to caudal, gradually locking joints and immobilising the patient
Involvement of the chest wall and paraspinal tissues produces thoracic insufficiency, the leading cause of premature death
Diagnosis is clinical, recognising the toe malformation and characteristic flare-ups, and is confirmed by ACVR1 molecular testing while avoiding provocative procedures
reference.pathophysiology: Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva is caused by an activating variant in ACVR1, a receptor in the bone morphogenetic protein signalling pathway. The mutant receptor becomes inappropriately responsive, including to activin, and drives excessive signalling that converts connective-tissue progenitor cells into cartilage and then bone through endochondral ossification. Inflammatory flare-ups, often after tissue injury, seed episodes of heterotopic ossification in muscle, tendon, ligament, and fascia. The accumulating extraskeletal bone bridges joints and restricts the chest wall, producing progressive immobility and life-limiting thoracic insufficiency.
additionalDifferentials: Osteosarcoma or other soft-tissue tumour (when flares are mistaken for masses)
Lymphoedema or soft-tissue infection during acute flares
additionalInvestigations: Clinical recognition of the malformed great toes and typical flare pattern
ACVR1 molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis
Imaging to map established heterotopic ossification while avoiding provocative procedures
Baseline and periodic respiratory and thoracic function assessment
Dental and airway planning to avoid mandibular and jaw ossification triggers
redFlags: New chest-wall or paraspinal ossification with declining respiratory reserve
Rapidly progressive flare-ups following trauma or an invasive procedure
Jaw ossification threatening oral intake and airway access
Falls in an immobilised patient, given high fracture and complication risk
reference.prognosis: The condition is relentlessly progressive, with cumulative loss of mobility and joint ankylosis; median survival is reduced, and thoracic insufficiency from chest-wall ossification is the usual cause of death. Avoiding iatrogenic triggers is central to limiting progression.
pitfalls: Performing a biopsy or intramuscular injection on a flare, which accelerates ossification
Misdiagnosing early flares as tumour, infection, or injury
Overlooking the diagnostic great-toe malformation at birth
Failing to plan carefully around dental and anaesthetic procedures
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: Strictly avoid iatrogenic triggers, withholding muscle biopsy, intramuscular injections, elective surgery on heterotopic bone and unnecessary trauma
Use a short course of corticosteroids for early flare-ups affecting major joints or the jaw to limit inflammatory oedema
Manage flares symptomatically with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, other anti-inflammatory measures and pain control
Consider disease-specific therapy with the retinoic acid receptor gamma agonist palovarotene or other ACVR1-directed agents to reduce heterotopic ossification under specialist care
Provide fall prevention, mobility aids and occupational therapy to protect against injury-induced ossification and preserve function
Undertake respiratory and thoracic surveillance for restrictive chest-wall disease and thoracic insufficiency
Plan dental and airway care carefully using non-traumatic techniques and avoiding mandibular block injections
Offer genetic counselling given the autosomal dominant ACVR1 variant, which usually arises de novo
